title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Oslo: find routes fast!
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra slice through Oslo’s street graph by running two synchronized shortest-path searches—one from the start and one from the goal. When the frontiers meet, the algorithm stitches together the optimal path with dramatically less work than a single-source run.
ig_caption:
🧭🚦 Oslo street graph, but make it algorithmic: today we visualize **Bidirectional Dijkstra**!

🔁 How it works (the deep stuff): instead of expanding only from the source, we run **two Dijkstra searches simultaneously**—one forward from the start node and one backward from the target node (using the directed/weighted road graph). Each side maintains its own priority queue and distance labels, and the search keeps progressing until the two explored regions **meet**. At the meeting point(s), we combine distances to form the candidate shortest path and can stop early using the best-known upper bound—often reducing explored nodes dramatically compared to classic Dijkstra.

🗺️ Graph theory meets real maps: intersections become **nodes**, road segments become **weighted edges** (distance, travel time, or cost). Because edges have nonnegative weights, Dijkstra’s optimality holds; bidirectional search leverages the symmetry of shortest paths to shrink the search horizon.

📚 This is a classic graph search idea: nodes = intersections, edges = road segments with nonnegative weights. If you’re learning algorithms, share this with a friend who loves coding visuals—and tell us what city we should visualize next!
